chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 261 to 270, Kapilar's kurinji decade on the boar: each poem opens on the boar of the hill (grazing the millet, keeping its mate, rearing motherless young, fighting the tiger, rooting the slope like a plough) and turns to the hill lord, through the heroine's doubts of his courage and love, her pallor and tears, his flattery and leaving, to his return at the harvest's end.

261.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the hill lord, of the land where the fierce-eyed boar that grazed the soft millet sleeps on the hard rock slope, stays away for fear that her father will find out, and concludes that this must be why he does not come.
261.nuance: The excuse she finds for him is a reproach: the boar of his own land raids the guarded millet and then sleeps without fear, while he, she supposes, is afraid of her father.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet, the boar and the rock slope fix the hill land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; எந்தை (my father) fixes the speaker as the heroine, and the secret love as the stage

iraicchi.act: the boar eats from the guarded millet field and then sleeps unafraid on the rock slope
iraicchi.sense: the beast of his own hill dares the guarded field and rests without fear, yet the man she loves stays away for fear of her father

262.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the love of the lord of the shining mountain, where the fierce-eyed boar that grazed the small millet stays with its mate on the slope of piled rocks, knows that his coming is the one remedy for her.
262.nuance: The whole sickness is turned into a question about his knowledge: his love may be real, but it does not seem to know the one medicine it could give, which is simply to come.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet, the boar and the boulder slope fix the hill land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; the vocative தோழி and her sickness that only his coming can cure fix the speaker

iraicchi.act: after feeding, the boar stays with its mate on the rock slope
iraicchi.sense: the boar keeps its mate's company, while the man stays away from the woman whose only cure is his coming

263.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the lord of the hill land, where a boar dark as a touchstone eats the ripened millet golden as fine gold, has come himself, and with him her beauty has come back.
263.nuance: The two similes belong together: gold and the black touchstone on which gold is tried, so the boar on the golden field looks like gold drawn across the testing stone. The doubled verb (வந்தனன் வந்தன்று) makes his arrival and the return of her beauty a single event. A hidden reading of the boar as the lover enjoying ripe beauty would rest on a single match of mood, so it stays simile.

264.reading: The friend tells the lord of the slope bright with springs, where a boar with tusks like the young crescent unites with its sow dark as the kalam fruit, that she has seen it: the eyes of the woman he loves have turned pale.
264.nuance: கண்டிகும் (we have seen) makes the friend a witness, so the pallor is reported as evidence, not complaint.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; the vocative சிலம்ப and நீ நயந்தோள் (the one you love) fix the friend speaking to the man

iraicchi.sense: the beast of his hill unites with its own mate, while the man leaves the woman he loves to grow pale, so he should come and marry her

265.reading: The heroine says the lord of the hill land, where the boar with curved white tusks rears the striped young of the sow a tiger killed, has forgotten her, he who left her with their son bright as gold.
265.nuance: The animal reverses the human case exactly: there the father rears young whose mother is dead; here the mother is left with a son whose father lives and has gone.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; புதல்வனோடு என் நீத்தோனே (who left me with the son) fixes the wife speaking in married life; the addressee is inferred

iraicchi.act: the boar rears and protects the striped young whose mother the tiger killed
iraicchi.sense: even the boar guards its motherless young, yet the man has forgotten and left his wife and son

266.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the great-tempered small-eyed boar fights the short-armed great tiger that they are surely bound by great modesty, but the eyes of the woman he loves have filled with tears.
266.nuance: The modesty is the reason they cannot speak or send for him, so the tears speak instead. The boar-and-tiger fight could be read as the dangers of his night path or as a clash he should take on, but the beasts do nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene.

267.reading: The heroine says that the lord of the hill land, where the great-tempered small-eyed boar drives off the bowmen on the boulder slope and carries off the mountain rice, fondles her bee-swarmed hair and speaks unworthy words, thinking she will believe them.
267.nuance: தேறுதல் செத்து (thinking it reassurance) shows she sees through him: the sweet words are taken for a pledge only by him.

268.reading: The heroine asks what the parting of the lord of the good hill can bring, now that he has left and abandoned them, the hill where the boar sleeps on the high peak with a striped young that has lost its mother, after eating the hunters' small millet.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; நம் (us) and his leaving fix the heroine speaking; the friend could also speak for both

iraicchi.act: the boar keeps the motherless young with it while it sleeps
iraicchi.sense: even the boar does not leave the young that has lost its mother, so the man's leaving her can bring nothing good

269.reading: The friend tells the heroine that if the lord of the land, where the reed sprung up from the boar's rooting shows like a crop in a ripened field, stays on there and does not come while she weeps, then by her own folly she will lose her companion.
269.nuance: The friend blames her own மடமை: she helped the secret love along, and now fears losing the friend to grief. The reed that rises in the boar's furrow looks like a crop nobody sowed, as the love grew unplanned.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; நீ அழ (while you weep) and the address by bangle and hair fix the friend speaking to the heroine

270.reading: The friend tells the heroine that, though the hunters have reaped the first crop from the slope the root-digging boar ploughed and gone, and the hill has grown bare and its high peak lonely, their lover, guessing their weeping sickness, has come himself.
270.nuance: With the harvest in, the millet watch is over and the girl is kept at home, so the bare hill is the end of their meeting place; his coming unbidden answers the fear that the season's end would end the love.

links.note: In Natrinai 386 the great-tempered boar that gorges on the hunters' millet and sleeps unafraid of the tiger frames a man who offers the dread oath and comes to wed; in Ainkurunuru 261 the boar that has grazed the millet and sleeps on the rock slope frames a man the heroine suspects of fearing her father.
links.teaches: The fearless sleeping boar was a stock frame whose point turns on the man set beside it, matching the bold suitor in Natrinai and shaming the timid one in Ainkurunuru, so the same image can carry praise or an unspoken reproach.

links.note: Both are spoken by the woman about the pallor that the man's presence will remove: Kural 1265 wishes to see him and says the pallor will then leave; Ainkurunuru 263 says he has come and her beauty has come back.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem gives as an accomplished fact, in two verbs set side by side, what the couplet can only promise, showing the restored beauty as the very event of his arrival rather than its later result.

links.note: The two poems close on nearly the same words to the hill lord about the eyes of the woman he loves: in 264 they have yielded pallor, in 266 tears (பனி), after the friend owns their great modesty.
links.teaches: Read in order, the decade escalates the friend's case for marriage from pallor to weeping by changing one word, while the boar beside it changes from mating with its sow to fighting a tiger.

links.note: Both are Kapilar's: in Akananuru 248 a boar holding a narrow pass to guard its young is spared by a hunter who sees in it his own chief holding the path; in Ainkurunuru 265 a boar rears the young of a sow the tiger killed, beside a man who left his wife and son.
links.teaches: Kapilar's boar guarding its young is a model of protection that even the hunter honours as heroic, which makes the husband of Ainkurunuru 265 fail a standard that both the beast and the hunter keep.

links.note: Both set a boar with a striped young that has lost its mother beside a man who has left: in 265 the boar rears it after a tiger killed the sow, in 268 it sleeps with it on the peak.
links.teaches: Taken together the pair fixes the reading of the motherless young in 268 by the tiger-killed sow named in 265, and shows the decade using one creature's care twice, once against a husband and once against a lover.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 267 opens with the same boar formula as Natrinai 386 (சிறுகண் பன்றிப் பெருஞ்சின ஒருத்தல்); Natrinai's boar sleeps unafraid after raiding the millet, Ainkurunuru's drives off the bowmen to seize the hill rice, beside a man whose words are not to be trusted.
links.teaches: One formula line for the raiding boar served poets for opposite men, the suitor who swears and weds and the one who flatters without pledge, so the boar's daring is admired or suspected according to what the man goes on to do.

links.note: Both open on the earth a boar has ploughed: in 269 a wild reed rises there like a crop and the friend fears the lord will stay away; in 270 the hunters reap the first crop from it and the lord comes of himself.
links.teaches: The decade ends by answering the friend's fear on the same boar-tilled ground, where the field that bore only a wild reed now yields a harvest and his return, so the image tracks whether the love will bear fruit.

links.note: Purananuru 168 praises Kotran's hill, where hill people sow millet unploughed in the earth a boar has turned and feast on the first new grain; in Ainkurunuru 270 the hunters reap the first crop from the boar-ploughed slope and leave the hill bare.
links.teaches: The same unploughed tillage and first harvest is plenty and hospitality in the praise of a patron but, for lovers who met at the millet watch, the end of their season and a bare hill, so akam reads the hill's farming calendar as a calendar of meeting.

source_issues: 261-270: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.
267 line 1: பறிப் stands for பன்றிப் (a lost ன்), unflagged; the same formula line reads சிறுகண் பன்றிப் பெருஞ்சின in 266 and in Natrinai 386. Marked as பன்றி.
261, 264, 265, 266, 268, 269, 270: lines repaired per the text flags; the marks follow the repaired lines.
265 line 1: புலிகொல் பெண்பால் is read as the sow killed by a tiger, whose young the boar rears; a reading with the tigress as killer is possible, so marked uncertain.
262 line 4, 266 line 4, 269 lines 3-5, 270 lines 3-4: the construction is open to more than one reading; marked uncertain.
